blocks.heading: Trade patterns and external accounts
blocks.text:
International trade is the buying and selling (exchange) of goods and services between countries. Exports are sales of goods or services to buyers abroad, while imports are purchases from abroad. Namibia’s main exports include minerals (especially diamonds and uranium), fish, beef and other farm products, and South Africa is its largest source of imports, which include fuel, vehicles, machinery and processed food. A change in world mineral prices therefore strongly affects Namibia’s export earnings. Patterns can change in product composition, trading partners or values over time. A rise in the money value of exports may reflect quantity, price or exchange effects, so it should not automatically be described as more physical output. State the measure and period before explaining the change. Product demand, production capacity, costs and international conditions can influence those patterns.

The goods balance is goods export value minus goods import value. In a period, exports N$90 million and imports N$110 million give a goods deficit of N$20 million. This is not the entire balance of payments. Services, relevant income and transfers as well as financial flows concern other international transactions. Investment funds entering an economy are not a service export simply because money arrives from abroad. A foreign investor financing a new workshop and a foreign customer paying for a repair service are different transactions. The balance of payments records all transactions with the rest of the world. The current account includes trade in goods (visible trade: visible exports − visible imports = the balance of trade), trade in services such as tourism, transport and insurance (invisible trade), primary income (wages, interest, profit and dividends) and secondary income (current transfers such as grants). The capital and financial account records investment and loan flows, such as a foreign firm building a factory. A current-account deficit means more is paid out than received on these items, and it is financed by borrowing, investment inflows or the country’s reserves. A wider external assessment needs the relevant accounts and financing evidence rather than treating a goods deficit as the whole result. An export pattern can change even if the overall goods balance stays the same. For instance, a decline in one product’s receipts may be offset by another’s rise. The composition matters to exposure and capacity even when the net number is unchanged. A description should therefore use the disaggregated information supplied, while a causal explanation links product demand or supply to the relevant change.

blocks.heading: Changing exchange rates
blocks.text:
An exchange rate expresses one currency’s value in another. Under market determination, a higher demand for a currency relative to its supply can raise its value, while a larger relative supply can lower it. Buyers of exports may need the exporter’s currency, and residents purchasing imports may supply domestic currency to obtain foreign money. Financial investment, interest incentives and expectations can also affect currency demand and supply. Reasons for fluctuations include changes in demand for exports and imports; tourism (foreign tourists must buy the currency); interest-rate differences that attract or repel investment funds; relative inflation (higher local inflation makes exports less competitive); speculation; and central-bank buying or selling of currency. Because the Namibia dollar is pegged one-to-one to the rand, it rises and falls with the rand against currencies such as the US dollar and the euro. An appreciation makes exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper; a depreciation tends to do the opposite (see 2.3).

For a market-determined currency, greater foreign demand for local products may increase currency demand if transactions require conversion. The resulting appreciation is conditional on the other influences, not a guaranteed response of every rate. A rise in relative interest returns may attract funds where risk and expectations support it, but investors make their own decisions. Namibia’s N$/rand parity is an institutional arrangement described in topic 2.3, so these market examples should not be read as a freely floating bilateral N$/rand forecast. A depreciation can raise domestic costs of unchanged foreign-priced imports. Whether it improves the current account depends on sufficiently responsive trade demand and whether supply can respond, as well as time and input costs. Keep the rate quote and response conditions visible. A quotation should be read before interpreting appreciation or depreciation. More domestic currency per foreign unit means the domestic unit is weaker against that foreign currency, not stronger because the printed number is larger. Foreign units per domestic unit use the opposite quotation direction. Topic 2.3 develops conversion; here the reason for a fluctuation must be kept separate from the arithmetic description of it.

blocks.heading: Two advantage tests
blocks.text:
Absolute advantage compares production efficiency using a common resource basis. Comparative advantage compares the alternative output forgone per unit. A side can be better at producing both goods in absolute terms yet still have a higher opportunity cost in one. The distinction explains why looking only at who makes more of everything does not settle the opportunity-cost pattern.

Use two producers with the same resource allocation. Producer A can make either 30 cloth units or 15 grain units; B can make either 12 cloth or 12 grain. These are alternative maxima, not simultaneous output. A has absolute advantage in both because 30 exceeds 12 and 15 exceeds 12. But A’s cloth costs 15/30=0.5 grain per cloth, compared with B’s 12/12=1. A has comparative advantage in cloth. A’s grain costs 30/15=2 cloth per grain, while B’s costs 1, so B has comparative advantage in grain. The ratios identify the good forgone and the good produced; a number without these units can be inverted accidentally.

blocks.heading: Gains and limits
blocks.text:
With different opportunity costs, specialisation and exchange can create potential gains under suitable terms. In the example, exchanging one cloth for 0.75 grain lies between the cloth opportunity costs 0.5 and 1 grain. A receives more grain for its cloth than its own forgone grain, while B obtains cloth for less grain than producing it itself would require. The calculation illustrates a possible mutually beneficial exchange, not a prediction of actual national trade terms.

Transport, quality, adjustment and other resource costs can reduce or offset gains. Resources may not move immediately between uses, and dependence on a narrow activity can create risks. A supported judgement states the feasible production and trade assumptions. This links to opportunity cost in 1.1 and specialisation in 1.3. Absolute output differences, comparative ratios, transaction flows and a country’s wider external position are related questions, but they are not interchangeable measures.

The importance of international trade. Benefits: access to goods a country cannot produce, such as some fuels and machinery; wider choice and often lower prices; larger markets that allow economies of scale; foreign-currency earnings; jobs in export industries; and gains from specialising according to comparative advantage. Drawbacks: dependence on a few exports or on one main supplier; competition from imports that can close local firms and cut jobs; exposure to world price and exchange-rate changes; and possible balance-of-payments deficits.
